How the stress model works: ODIS stores every indicator as a 0–100 stress score (higher = more stress). For broadband and healthcare, the score is the share of households or children without access — so broadband = 21 means 21% of households lack broadband. Park access, violent crime, and SNAP are similarly higher-is-worse. Each intervention lowers its indicator score. Stress removed per point uses ODIS's own formula: the composite is the average of five domains (Economic, Education, Health, Housing, Crime), and each domain is the average of its indicators. One point of violent crime moves the composite by 1/5 × 1/2 = 0.10; park access by 1/5 × 1/3 ≈ 0.067; broadband by 1/5 × 1/4 = 0.05; healthcare and SNAP by 1/5 × 1/5 = 0.04. When a school is missing data, weights are recalculated using only present indicators. The composite is rescaled so the lowest-stress school = 0 and the highest = 100 (raw scores run from 9 to 63). Levers are recommended for schools above the national median for that indicator (broadband >20%, healthcare >5%, park access >40, violent crime >30, SNAP >47). Each lever is capped at the national 90th-percentile benchmark — no school is modelled as surpassing what the top 10% already achieves. "Build cheapest plan" fills the most cost-efficient lever first and caps any single lever at 40% of the target. Composite scores never go below 0.

How cost estimates work: Cost = points lowered × base cost per point × a combined county multiplier. The multiplier has two components: (1) a population scaler = √(county population ÷ 85,000), held between 0.5× and 3×, reflecting that larger communities require larger program budgets; and (2) a regional price adjustment using the Bureau of Economic Analysis Regional Price Parity (RPP) index by state (national average = 100). These are multiplied together, so a large county in an expensive state has a higher multiplier than a small county in a low-cost state.

Base cost sources (national averages per 1-point improvement in the ODIS indicator):

InterventionBase cost / ptSource & derivation
🌳 Park access$400,000Trust for Public Land City Park Facts 2024; Tracy CA Parks Master Plan 2022 — 5-acre neighborhood park costs ~$5.4M, walkshed covers ~2,000 people. ODIS uses school attendance boundaries averaging 8,000–15,000 people, so one park improves the score by ~13–25 pts ($216K–$405K/pt). Using $400K as a conservative midpoint.
📶 Broadband$120,000Affordability subsidy approach: ~$120/yr per household × ~1,000 households per 1 ODIS point (annual ongoing cost). Fiber build-out alternative: ~$1.1M/pt (Cartesian/FBA Fiber Deployment Cost Annual Report 2024: $10,800–$13,100 per unserved location × ~100 households/pt). ODIS measures subscriptions; much of the gap is affordability, not infrastructure absence.
🏥 Healthcare$320,000Insurance enrollment assistance model. ODIS healthcare measures share of children aged 6–18 with health insurance — not care access — so mobile clinics do not move this indicator. Cost based on ~$2,400 per extra insured child (parent mentor enrollment model) × ~130 children per 1 ODIS point.
🚔 Violent crime$90,000DOJ Community Violence Intervention grants 2022–23; Healthy Communities for Youth cost analysis (Prevention Science, 2024) — $821K over 34 months; $8,100 per youth violent crime case avoided. Note: the study's crime reduction was not statistically significant.
🍎 SNAP dependency$700,000Reducing SNAP dependency requires addressing underlying poverty through income support (e.g. EITC expansion), not outreach. Outreach increases SNAP uptake and would raise the ODIS stress score — the opposite direction. Cost based on ~$700K/yr per point via income-support programs.

All base costs reflect national averages and are adjusted by the county multiplier described above. Actual costs vary substantially by site conditions, existing infrastructure, and contractor market. These estimates are intended for comparative planning, not procurement. Each lever is capped at the national 90th-percentile benchmark for that indicator (10th percentile of the stress score, since lower = better) — so no school is assumed to surpass what the top 10% of US schools already achieves. Targets in ODIS stress-score terms: park access → 4, broadband → 9, healthcare → 2, violent crime → 8, SNAP dependency → 31. Derived from the ODIS 2026 national distribution (n ≈ 23,000 schools). Schools already at or below a target get a cap of 0 for that lever. Regional price adjustment uses BEA Regional Price Parities 2022 (official release); Puerto Rico uses the national average (100) as BEA does not publish an RPP for Puerto Rico. The population factor is clamped to 0.5–3× before multiplying.

Index data: Hawken, Minar, Choudhary & Kulick (2026), Open Data Index for Schools (ODIS), Johns Hopkins Research Data Repository, doi:10.7281/T170WN53, CC BY 4.0. RPP data: Bureau of Economic Analysis Table SARPP, 2022.

County boundaries: US Census cartographic boundary file via Plotly datasets. County populations: 2019 Census Bureau estimates via the Johns Hopkins CSSE FIPS lookup table; edit the population above to use a newer figure.
